correctness.rationale: Stable deterministic roots r_s,r_f<0 give unique stochastic-convolution invariant marginal with L^alpha kernel. u=e^(-Delta*t/m) gives beta scale and gamma ratio exactly. Digamma integral and strict sinh convexity prove H'(a)>0 for every a>=0 and 1<alpha<2. At m_c the repeated-root response yields the gamma endpoint. Because both invariant marginals are the same centered stable law at different positive scales, the common-Z coupling and 1-Lipschitz |x| test attain identical W1, not just a bound. Expansion a=alpha*kappa*m/gamma^2+O(m^2) gives exact C_alpha>0, with sign inherited from H'(0)>0. The standard-library numerical checks pass 197 finite assertions and are not used in place of infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The stationary stable-kernel representation and oscillator impulse formula are explicitly prior mathematics (Dybiec et al., 2017). The target new implication is all-mass strict inflation of the stationary position scale for non-Gaussian 1<alpha<2 throughout 0<m<=gamma^2/(4*kappa), plus an exact nonzero linear W1 small-mass constant. Jin–Tao (2026), Theorem 1.2, supplies only a general O(m^(1/alpha)) comparison; Baldovin et al. (2022) supplies Fourier-space stationary descriptions but not this mass ordering or derivative. A nontrivial gamma-ratio sign calculation and matched W1 bounds establish the extra conclusions. No priority is asserted for general gamma-ratio inequalities themselves. The full-combination novelty remains best-knowledge, requiring external priority review.

value.rationale: The 2026 literature motivates obtaining quantitative stationary small-mass approximation rates under stable noise. On its canonical harmonic benchmark, the theorem identifies a strict signed response throughout every nonoscillatory mass and a sharp, strictly positive O(m) scale, significantly different from the published general O(m^(1/alpha)) estimate. The exact W1 formula and Gaussian vs non-Gaussian contrast clarify which effects are caused by stable tails rather than drift nonlinearity; this is a natural structural classification, not an arbitrary numerical slice.
